The relevant axis is the structure imposed on the restriction maps.
2.3 Sheaf Attention

2.4 Restriction Map Families

The restriction maps \mathcal{F}_{i\trianglelefteq e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} ℱi​⊴​e∈ℝd×d\mathcal{F}_{i\trianglelefteq e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} can be organized into a hierarchy of increasingly general parameterizations (Bodnar et al. 2022):

\mathcal{F}_{i\trianglelefteq e} ℱi​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{i\trianglelefteq e} is diagonal, scaling each stalk coordinate independently. This parametrization has fewest parameters and stalk dimensions interact only through the left multiplication by {W}_{1} W1{W}_{1}.

Orthogonal maps mix stalk dimensions while preserving norms, regularize via fewer free parameters ( d(d-1)/2 d⁡(d−1)/2d(d-1)/2), and yield Laplacians that are numerically convenient to normalize.

4 Sheaf Models and Inductive Implementation

Throughout, d dd is the stalk dimension, f ff the channels per stalk, c=df c=d​fc=df the per-node representation size. Node-level tasks feed the node-stalk representations to a per-node head, while graph-level tasks first pool them with a permutation-invariant readout before the head. Our study is organized around a two-dimensional design space: three diffusion mechanisms that propagate information and three restriction-map parameterizations (and dimensions) that transport features between stalks. The two axes are orthogonal, so their combination forms a 3\times 3 3×33\times 3 grid, one row of which is a new sheaf-attention layer we introduce. We first define the grid, then propose a Laplacian-free implementation for any diffusion mechanism that makes it trainable under cross-graph batching, introduce our dynamic sheaf-attention mechanism, derive the complexity, and define how modern GNN components are combined with the inductive sheaf operator (Fig. 1-Top-left).
The Sheaf Design Space.

The three diffusion mechanisms analyzed in this study share the sheaf transport block {P}_{ij}=\mathcal{F}_{i\trianglelefteq e}^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{j\trianglelefteq e} Pi​j=ℱi​⊴​e⊤​ℱj​⊴​e{P}_{ij}=\mathcal{F}_{i\trianglelefteq e}^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{j\trianglelefteq e}, the mixing matrices {W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} W1∈ℝd×d{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and {W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times f} W2∈ℝf×f{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times f}, the intrinsic nonlinearity \sigma σ\sigma, and a residual connection. They differ in how neighbor messages are weighted. NSD propagates through the learnable normalized sheaf Laplacian of Eq. (2), so every neighbor contributes through the transport alone. SAN and our newly proposed SANv2 instead modulate the transport with input-dependent attention, and differ from each other in how the attention scores are computed: statically for SAN, dynamically for SANv2. Because the restriction maps set {P}_{ij} Pi​j{P}_{ij} while the attention coefficients set the weighting, how features are transported between stalks stays decoupled from how strongly each neighbor contributes. Each mechanism is paired with one of the three restriction-map families seen in Sec. 2 (Diag, O(d), Gen), giving nine models. With all else fixed, this grid isolates two questions prior work conflates: (1) whether restriction-map type or diffusion mechanism dominates, and (2) whether they interact, that is, whether the best map family depends on the mechanism and the reverse.

Complexity.

Per layer per graph, restriction-map prediction dominates at \mathcal{O}(m\,d^{3}f) 𝒪⁡(m​d3​f)\mathcal{O}(m\,d^{3}f) for O( d dd)/Gen and \mathcal{O}(m\,d^{2}f) 𝒪⁡(m​d2​f)\mathcal{O}(m\,d^{2}f) for Diag; transport and aggregation add \mathcal{O}(m\,d^{2}f) 𝒪⁡(m​d2​f)\mathcal{O}(m\,d^{2}f); degree blocks and their inverse square roots add \mathcal{O}((n+m)\,d^{3}) 𝒪⁡((n+m)​d3)\mathcal{O}((n+m)\,d^{3}). In total,

\displaystyle\text{Time:} Time:\displaystyle\text{Time:} \displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\left(n+m\right)\,d^{2}f+m\,d^{3}f\right) 𝒪⁡((n+m)​d2​f+m​d3​f)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\left(n+m\right)\,d^{2}f+m\,d^{3}f\right) (11) \displaystyle\text{Space:} Space:\displaystyle\text{Space:} \displaystyle\mathcal{O}\big(m\,d^{2}+(n+m)\,df\big), 𝒪⁡(m​d2+(n+m)​d​f),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\big(m\,d^{2}+(n+m)\,df\big),

both linear in n nn and m mm. No operator is assembled or factorized, and the edge-wise pass composes with PyTorch Geometric batching, so a batch of graphs is one disjoint union processed without a per-graph loop. This is what makes our sheaf models trainable in the inductive, graph-batched regime the reference implementation does not support.
